advances: Proves the sharp finite-set bound \(\lvert A\rvert\leq\binom{2d+1}{d}<4^d\) under the requested arithmetic-mean and unique-interior-lattice-point hypotheses. Powers of an adapted product yield the bound directly in the original dimension. The argument requires only the infinitude of primes, proved below. The capacity composition is not part of this statement.
author: research-agent
external_sources: Initio Intelligence, Inc., [Ehrhart's sharp volume bound](https://initiointelligence.com/papers/Ehrhart_full_proof.pdf), August 5, 2026, updated August 10, 2026. The update is identified on the title page as a correction to Lemma 5. Sections 2, 4 (especially Lemma 5), and 6 motivate the Taylor filtration, simultaneous basis elimination, and characteristic-\(p\) quotient. Every algebraic statement needed here is proved above. Taking powers of the product permits the use of arbitrary sufficiently large primes, whose existence is proved above, and leads to the finite binomial extraction. No continuous-volume theorem or prime-interval theorem from the source is assumed.
proof:
Put \(P=\operatorname{conv}A\) and \(M=\lvert A\rvert\). In particular \(0\in\operatorname{int}P\) and \(M\geq d+1\). For \(0\leq\lambda<1\), convexity gives \(\lambda P\subseteq\operatorname{int}P\): choose \(\varepsilon>0\) so that \(\varepsilon B\subseteq P\), where \(B\) is the Euclidean unit ball; for each \(x\in P\), the set \(\lambda x+(1-\lambda)\varepsilon B\) is a neighborhood of \(\lambda x\) contained in \(P\). Consequently, if \(q>r>0\) and \(v\in\mathbb Z^d\) satisfy \(qv\in rP\), then \(v\in(r/q)P\subseteq\operatorname{int}P\), so \(v=0\).

Fix a prime \(p\). Work in the Laurent polynomial ring \(R_p=\mathbb F_p[z_1^{\pm1},\ldots,z_d^{\pm1}]\) and its \(M\)-dimensional subspace \(V=\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb F_p}\{z^a:a\in A\}\), where \(z^a=\prod_{i=1}^d z_i^{a_i}\). This construction precedes any quotient by \(z_i^p-1\): distinct integer exponent vectors give linearly independent Laurent monomials over every \(\mathbb F_p\).

Substitution \(z_i=1+y_i\) defines a homomorphism \(E:R_p\longrightarrow\mathbb F_p[[y_1,\ldots,y_d]]\), because every \(1+y_i\) is a unit. It is injective. Indeed, for a nonzero Laurent polynomial \(f\), choose a monomial \(z^v\) such that \(z^vf\) is a polynomial. Polynomial substitution \(z_i\mapsto1+y_i\) is invertible, so \(E(z^vf)\neq0\); since \(E(z^v)\) is a unit, \(E(f)\neq0\). For nonzero \(f\), let \(\operatorname{ord}(f)\) be the least total degree of a nonzero term of \(E(f)\). The lowest-degree homogeneous parts multiply in the domain \(\mathbb F_p[y_1,\ldots,y_d]\), giving \(\operatorname{ord}(fg)=\operatorname{ord}(f)+\operatorname{ord}(g)\).

The orders of nonzero elements of \(V\) are uniformly bounded. To see this, choose a single monomial \(z^v\) so that all elements of \(z^vV\) are polynomials of bounded total degree. Their substitutions have the same degree bound, while multiplication by \(E(z^v)\), a unit of order \(0\), preserves order. Thus the decreasing subspaces \(V_j=\{0\}\cup\{f\in V\setminus\{0\}:\operatorname{ord}(f)\geq j\}\), for integers \(j\geq0\), satisfy \(V_0=V\) and \(V_j=0\) for all sufficiently large \(j\).

For \(j\geq1\), the space \(V_j\) is the kernel of the linear map recording the coefficients of \(E(f)\) in total degree less than \(j\). There are \(\binom{d+j-1}{d}\) such coefficients. With \((x)_+=\max\{x,0\}\), this gives

\[
\dim_{\mathbb F_p}V_j\geq
\left(M-\binom{d+j-1}{d}\right)_+,
\qquad
\sum_{j\geq1}\dim_{\mathbb F_p}V_j\geq
\mathcal L:=\sum_{j\geq1}\left(M-\binom{d+j-1}{d}\right)_+.
\]

The number \(\mathcal L\) is finite and depends only on \(d,M\), not on \(p\).

We next construct a basis of \(V\) adapted both to this filtration and to a monomial order. First, a basis adapted to the filtration exists: choose a complement of \(V_{j+1}\) in \(V_j\) for each \(j\geq0\), and take the union of bases of these complements. Every chosen vector in the \(j\)-th complement has order exactly \(j\). Thus for every \(j\), the basis vectors of order at least \(j\) form a basis of \(V_j\).

Choose a real linear functional \(\ell\) that takes distinct values on \(A\); avoiding the finitely many hyperplanes \(\ell(a-b)=0\) for distinct \(a,b\in A\) gives such a functional. The pivot of a nonzero element of \(V\) is its supported exponent with smallest \(\ell\)-value. Starting with an adapted basis, suppose two distinct basis vectors \(f,g\) have the same pivot. Interchange their names if necessary so that \(\operatorname{ord}(f)\leq\operatorname{ord}(g)\). Subtract the appropriate nonzero scalar multiple of \(g\) from \(f\) to cancel their common pivot, replacing \(f\) by \(f'=f-cg\). This is an elementary basis operation, so \(f'\neq0\) and the resulting vectors remain a basis.

The order of \(f'\) is at least that of \(f\), and it cannot be larger. If it were larger, set \(j=\operatorname{ord}(f)+1\). All original basis vectors of order at least \(j\) are unchanged, since \(f\) was not one of them. They are \(\dim V_j\) independent vectors in \(V_j\), and the new basis would add the independent vector \(f'\in V_j\), a contradiction. Hence the order of every basis vector is unchanged by this operation. The new basis is still adapted: for each \(j\) it has exactly \(\dim V_j\) independent vectors in \(V_j\).

Both \(f\) and \(g\) had no supported exponent preceding their shared pivot, so the pivot of \(f'\) strictly follows it in the ordering of \(A\) by \(\ell\). Number the elements of \(A\) by the ranks \(1,\ldots,M\) in this ordering. Each operation strictly increases the sum of the \(M\) pivot ranks, an integer bounded above by \(M^2\). Repetition therefore terminates with an adapted basis \(f_1,\ldots,f_M\) whose pivots are distinct. These pivots exhaust \(A\).

Let \(F=\prod_{i=1}^M f_i\). Adaptation and additivity of order give

\[
\operatorname{ord}(F)
=\sum_{i=1}^M\operatorname{ord}(f_i)
=\sum_{j\geq1}\#\{i:\operatorname{ord}(f_i)\geq j\}
=\sum_{j\geq1}\dim V_j
\geq\mathcal L.
\]

If the pivot of \(f_i\) is \(a_i\), then \(\sum_i a_i=\sum_{a\in A}a=0\), as an equality of integer exponent vectors. For any choice \(b_i\in\operatorname{supp}(f_i)\), each \(\ell(b_i)\geq\ell(a_i)\), with equality only for \(b_i=a_i\). Therefore \(\ell(\sum_i b_i)\geq0\), and equality occurs only when every chosen exponent is a pivot. It follows that \(F\) has a nonzero constant coefficient, equal to the product of its factors' pivot coefficients, and that every other supported exponent has strictly positive \(\ell\)-value. Every exponent of \(F\) lies in \(MP\), since it is a sum of \(M\) elements of \(A\).

For every positive integer \(t\), these properties imply that \(F^t\) has a nonzero constant coefficient, that \(\operatorname{supp}(F^t)\subseteq tMP\), and that \(\operatorname{ord}(F^t)=t\operatorname{ord}(F)\geq t\mathcal L\). In particular, its constant coefficient is the \(t\)-th power of the constant coefficient of \(F\): any selection involving a nonzero supported exponent has positive total \(\ell\)-value and cannot contribute to exponent \(0\).

Now suppose \(p>M\), and choose \(t=\lfloor(p-1)/M\rfloor\geq1\), so \(tM<p\). Consider the quotient

\[
Q_p=R_p/(z_1^p-1,\ldots,z_d^p-1)
\cong\mathbb F_p[y_1,\ldots,y_d]/(y_1^p,\ldots,y_d^p).
\]

The isomorphism follows from \(z_i^p-1=(z_i-1)^p\) in characteristic \(p\) and \(z_i=1+y_i\); these images are units because \((1+y_i)^p=1\). In the Laurent presentation, the classes of \(z^u\) for \(u\in\{0,\ldots,p-1\}^d\) form a basis. Indeed, \(z_i^{-1}=z_i^{p-1}\) in the quotient, and ordinary division by the monic polynomials \(z_i^p-1\), successively in the \(d\) variables, gives unique representatives with degree less than \(p\) in each variable.

The coefficient of the residue-zero basis element in the image of \(F^t\) is the sum of its coefficients at exponents in \(p\mathbb Z^d\). The geometric observation at the start, with \(r=tM\) and \(q=p\), shows that \(tMP\cap p\mathbb Z^d=\{0\}\). Thus this coefficient is exactly the nonzero constant coefficient of \(F^t\), so its image in \(Q_p\) is nonzero.

On the other hand, every monomial surviving in the \(y\)-presentation of \(Q_p\) has degree at most \(d(p-1)\). The canonical quotient map from \(R_p\) agrees with Taylor expansion \(E\) followed by reduction modulo \((y_1^p,\ldots,y_d^p)\): both maps send each \(z_i\) to the same invertible element \(1+y_i\), which also determines the images of all negative powers. A Laurent polynomial of order greater than \(d(p-1)\) therefore has zero image in \(Q_p\). Nonvanishing of the image of \(F^t\) proves

\[
t\mathcal L\leq \operatorname{ord}(F^t)\leq d(p-1).
\]

Write \(p-1=tM+s\), where \(0\leq s<M\). Dividing by \(t\) yields \(\mathcal L\leq dM+d(M-1)/t\). There are arbitrarily large primes: a finite complete list of primes would fail to contain any prime divisor of one plus their product. Hence \(p\) can tend to infinity and \(t=\lfloor(p-1)/M\rfloor\) tends to infinity. Since \(\mathcal L\) is independent of \(p\), we conclude that \(\mathcal L\leq dM\).

The positive part of a real number is at least that number. Keeping the first \(d+1\) terms in the definition of \(\mathcal L\), and using Pascal's identity to telescope the binomial sum, we obtain

\[
\begin{aligned}
dM
&\geq\mathcal L\\
&\geq\sum_{j=1}^{d+1}\left(M-\binom{d+j-1}{d}\right)\\
&=(d+1)M-\binom{2d+1}{d+1}.
\end{aligned}
\]

Indeed, \(\sum_{j=1}^{d+1}\binom{d+j-1}{d}=\binom{2d+1}{d+1}\). Rearranging gives \(M\leq\binom{2d+1}{d}\). The binomial expansion of \(2^{2d+1}\) contains the two equal central terms \(\binom{2d+1}{d}\) and \(\binom{2d+1}{d+1}\), as well as other positive terms because \(d\geq1\). Hence \(2\binom{2d+1}{d}<2^{2d+1}\), proving the requested strict upper comparison with \(4^d\).

For sharpness, let \(P_\Delta=(d+1)\Delta_d-\mathbf1\) and \(A_\Delta=P_\Delta\cap\mathbb Z^d\). The inequalities of \(P_\Delta\) are \(a_i\geq-1\) for \(1\leq i\leq d\) and \(\sum_i a_i\leq1\). Its vertices belong to \(A_\Delta\), so \(\operatorname{conv}A_\Delta=P_\Delta\) is full dimensional. An interior integer point satisfies \(a_i\geq0\) and \(\sum_i a_i\leq0\), and therefore equals \(0\); conversely \(0\) is interior.

The map \(a\mapsto(b_0,b_1,\ldots,b_d)\), given by \(b_i=a_i+1\) for \(i\geq1\) and \(b_0=1-\sum_i a_i\), is a bijection from \(A_\Delta\) to the nonnegative integer vectors of length \(d+1\) whose coordinates sum to \(d+1\). The stars-and-bars count is \(\lvert A_\Delta\rvert=\binom{2d+1}{d}\). This set of vectors is invariant under permutations of its \(d+1\) coordinates. Consequently the sums of each coordinate over the set are equal; summing all these coordinate sums shows that each is \(\lvert A_\Delta\rvert\). Thus \(\sum_{a\in A_\Delta}a_i=\sum_{a\in A_\Delta}(b_i-1)=0\) for each \(i\). The set \(A_\Delta\) satisfies all hypotheses and attains the binomial bound.
statement:
Let \(d\geq1\) be an integer, and let \(A\subseteq\mathbb Z^d\) be a finite set of distinct vectors whose affine hull is \(\mathbb R^d\). Suppose that \(\sum_{a\in A}a=0\) and \(\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{conv}A)\cap\mathbb Z^d=\{0\}\). Then

\[
\lvert A\rvert\leq\binom{2d+1}{d}<4^d.
\]

The binomial bound is attained by \(A=((d+1)\Delta_d-\mathbf1)\cap\mathbb Z^d\), where \(\Delta_d=\operatorname{conv}\{0,e_1,\ldots,e_d\}\) and \(\mathbf1=(1,\ldots,1)\). There is no hypothesis that \(A\) contains \(0\), equals \(\operatorname{conv}(A)\cap\mathbb Z^d\), or has a convex hull with continuous centroid \(0\). No condition is imposed on the index of the subgroup generated by \(A-A\).
